The Download: testing tech promises and searching for cognitive immortality
Plus: Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia CEO.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Are we there yet? Six technologies that promised to change the world
How do you measure progress towards the future? In the Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, our series “Are we there yet?” examines how far six potentially transformative technologies have come after years of promises.
We spoke to experts, researchers and engineers to find out what’s holding them back, then scored each on a progress meter from zero to ten.  Find out how we rated each of these technologies—and how close they are to delivering on their promise.
Nuclear-powered spaceships
Exercise in a pill
Interspecies communication
Solid-state batteries
Cleaning up PFAS
Eliminating traffic deaths
Subscribe now to get every issue of our print magazine as soon as it lands.
Inside the quest for cognitive immortality
Could technology keep your brain going beyond death? Far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to make it happen, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores these ideas and how close they might be to reality.
Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado for this subscriber-only discussion tomorrow.
Tune in live on Tuesday, November 17 at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia CEO
He’s discussed with confidants the possibility of returning. (FT $)
+ Elon Musk has joined 165,000 signatories calling for his recall. (Guardian)
+ The Treasury Secretary wants them to hire an outsider. (Axios)
+ Megaspeed says the alleged China spy left the company last year. (BBC)
+ Trump plans to name Nvidia an AI “national champion.” (WSJ $)
+ Nvidia privately said it can track chips to China. (MIT Technology Review)
2 SpaceX has caught a rocket returning from orbit for the first time
The feat brings fully reusable rockets closer to reality. (Guardian)
+ The feat shows what audacious engineering can achieve. (Atlantic $)
+ Meanwhile, Ukraine says SpaceX is lying about Starshield speed restrictions. (Reuters $)
3 The US and allies have agreed to guard AI supply chains from China
Ten countries will collaborate to secure critical technologies. (FT $)
+ Chinese AI stocks have plunged on export control fears. (Information $)
+ Nvidia privately said it can track chips to China. (MIT Technology Review)
4 The US flight shutdown exposed weaknesses in air traffic technology
Officials blamed the disruption on a faulty router installation. (Reuters $)
+ It was a terrible week of outages. (WP $)
5 The first in-body CRISPR treatment is set to reach patients next year
The treatment could gain FDA approval as early as March. (Nature)
+ CRISPR has created female clones of male mice. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Congress plans to make data centers pay billions more for power
A proposed bill would shift grid costs onto tech companies. (NYT $)
+ Utilities also want tech giants to pay more for power. (Bloomberg $)
+ Is data center hatred all about electricity? (MIT Technology Review)
7 Apple plans to launch its first smart glasses next year
It’s betting on Siri to give the specs an edge. (Verge)
8 Bill Gates has made billions from climate-polluting landfills
His investment in a landfill operator is worth $29 billion. (ProPublica)
9 A new AI device turns everyday objects into needy virtual pets
The tiny gadgets aim to encourage healthier everyday habits. (Wired $)
10 Scientists made monkeys watch Minions to study their brains
Their findings challenge traditional vision models. (404 Media)
Quote of the day
“If our hopes for the future are pinned on any one individual being trustworthy, then we're pretty screwed.”
—Helen Toner, former OpenAI board member, tells The Verge that AI needs stronger governance than trusting tech executives to do the right thing.
One more thing
How AI and Wikipedia have sent vulnerable languages into a doom spiral
When Kenneth Wehr started managing the Greenlandic-language version of Wikipedia, he discovered that almost every article had been written by people who didn’t speak the language.
A growing number of them had been copy-pasted into Wikipedia from machine translators—and were riddled with elementary mistakes. This is beginning to cause a wicked problem.
AI systems, from Google Translate to ChatGPT, learn new languages by scraping text from Wikipedia. This could push the most vulnerable languages on Earth toward the precipice.
Read the full story on what happens when AI gets trained on junk pages.
—Jacob Judah
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ Adelaide Zoo is celebrating its first cassowary eggs in 34 years.
+ Photos fill the frame at the Epson Pano awards, which celebrate panoramic photography.
+ Indonesia has called an early halt to the world's largest deforestation project, saving up to 4 million acres.
+ After over a month on the loose in Yellowstone, a little dog called Luna has been reunited with her owners.
